reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: A subacute-to-chronic infection caused by the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix, acquired through traumatic inoculation of soil, thorns, sphagnum moss or plant material into the skin
The classic lymphocutaneous form begins as a papule or nodule at the inoculation site that ulcerates, followed by a chain of nodules tracking along lymphatic channels (sporotrichoid spread)
A fixed cutaneous form remains localised at the inoculation site without lymphatic progression
Occupational and recreational exposure among gardeners, farmers and forestry workers is a key historical clue
Extracutaneous disease, including osteoarticular, pulmonary and disseminated forms, occurs mainly in immunocompromised or alcoholic patients
Diagnosis is confirmed by fungal culture of pus, tissue or aspirate, with histopathology sometimes showing yeast forms and asteroid bodies

Itraconazole is the preferred agent for cutaneous and lymphocutaneous disease, with amphotericin-based therapy reserved for severe, disseminated or meningeal infection; saturated potassium iodide remains a low-cost option in some settings
reference.pathophysiology: Sporothrix species exist as mould in the environment and convert to a yeast form at body temperature after traumatic inoculation into skin or subcutaneous tissue. A localised suppurative and granulomatous (mixed pyogranulomatous) inflammatory response develops. The organism spreads proximally along lymphatic vessels, producing successive nodules. In immunocompromised hosts or after inhalation, haematogenous or pulmonary dissemination can occur, involving bones, joints, lungs and rarely the meninges. Cell-mediated immunity is central to containment, explaining severe disease in those with impaired T-cell function.
additionalInvestigations: Fungal culture of aspirate, exudate or tissue as the diagnostic gold standard
Histopathology of biopsy for granulomatous inflammation and yeast forms with asteroid bodies
Imaging of bone and joints when osteoarticular disease is suspected
Chest imaging in suspected pulmonary involvement
Assessment of immune status including HIV testing in disseminated disease
redFlags: Disseminated or multifocal disease suggesting significant immunosuppression
Pulmonary involvement with cavitation or systemic symptoms
Meningeal involvement, which is rare but serious and difficult to treat
reference.prognosis: Lymphocutaneous and fixed cutaneous disease respond well to prolonged azole therapy with an excellent outcome, whereas disseminated, pulmonary and meningeal forms carry a much poorer prognosis and require aggressive treatment, particularly in immunocompromised hosts.
pitfalls: Stopping antifungal therapy too early before lesions have fully resolved, risking relapse
Overlooking the inoculation history and misdiagnosing bacterial infection
Failing to investigate for immunosuppression in disseminated cases
Not distinguishing sporotrichoid spread from other causes of nodular lymphangitis
management: Itraconazole as first-line therapy for lymphocutaneous and fixed cutaneous disease, continued for weeks beyond clinical resolution
Amphotericin B for severe disseminated, pulmonary or meningeal disease, particularly in immunocompromised hosts, with step-down to itraconazole once stabilised
Saturated potassium iodide solution as an alternative for cutaneous disease where azoles are unsuitable or unavailable
Local hyperthermia as an option for cutaneous disease in pregnancy, where systemic antifungals are contraindicated
Surgical debridement or drainage as an adjunct in osteoarticular or cavitary pulmonary disease
Assess and optimise immune status, including HIV testing and management, given the risk of dissemination
Advise protective gloves and clothing during gardening, forestry and handling of soil or sphagnum moss to prevent re-inoculation
